title: Le scénario de Hartman  (Mathias and Isabelle)

segments.t: At a quiet restaurant in Paris, Mathias meets with superstar Isabelle Adjani to review an ambitious movie script. While Isabelle loves the dramatic depth of the project, Mathias cautiously warns her about the director's eccentric demands. Listen to the scene in French first.
C'est un scénario profond et intelligent.
C'est un art dramatique puissant.
C'est tout ce que j'aime.
C'est bien? Je vais conclure.
Vous devez savoir une chose importante.
Sacha Hartman n'est pas facile.
J'y suis habituée, tu sais.
Je peux être épuisante aussi.
Il fait chanter toute son équipe.
J'ai toujours adoré ta franchise.
S'il y a un problème, dis-le.
Hartman a choisi quelqu'un d'autre?
Andréa a été un peu vite.
Il pense à une actrice américaine.
Oui, bien sûr. C'est dommage.
Let's walk through the conversation step by step.
C'est un scénario profond et intelligent.
'It is a profound and intelligent screenplay.' Both describing words follow 'screenplay' in French, and 'profound' commonly means 'deep' in everyday speech.
C'est un art dramatique puissant.
'It is powerful dramatic art.' Putting two descriptions after 'art' — 'dramatic' then 'powerful' — gives Isabelle's praise rich theatrical weight in French.
C'est tout ce que j'aime.
'It is everything that I love.' Where English can say 'all I love', French bridges 'all' and 'I love' with 'that which' — never leaving that gap empty.
C'est bien? Je vais conclure.
'Is it good? I will close the deal.' In business talk, the cognate 'conclude' works on its own in French to mean 'close the deal'.
Vous devez savoir une chose importante.
'You must know an important thing.' Mathias keeps the formal 'you' here while Isabelle answers him with casual 'you', reflecting his old-school deference.
Sacha Hartman n'est pas facile.
'Sacha Hartman is not easy.' Calling a person 'not easy' works word-for-word in French to warn gently about a prickly temperament.
J'y suis habituée, tu sais.
'I am used to it, you know.' Putting a tiny word meaning 'to it' right after 'I' packs 'used to it' neatly before 'am accustomed' in French.
Je peux être épuisante aussi.
'I can be exhausting too.' Built from 'exhaust' or 'drain a well', the describing word sounds its final 't' when Isabelle describes herself.
Il fait chanter toute son équipe.
'He makes his entire crew sing.' Pairing 'makes' immediately with 'sing' ahead of 'his whole team' is how French builds 'makes someone do something'.
J'ai toujours adoré ta franchise.
'I have always loved your frankness.' Watch the false friend at the end: rather than a store chain, it means 'frankness' or 'candor' in French.
S'il y a un problème, dis-le.
'If there is a problem, say so.' Literally 'say-it', French attaches 'it' after a hyphen onto the command where English says 'say so'.
Hartman a choisi quelqu'un d'autre?
'Hartman chose someone else?' Linking 'someone' to 'other' requires a shortened 'of' in between in French — literally 'someone of other'.
Andréa a été un peu vite.
'Andrea was a bit too hasty.' Literally 'Andrea has been a little fast', French pairs 'been' with 'fast' to mean she jumped the gun.
Il pense à une actrice américaine.
'He is thinking of an American actress.' Thinking about someone takes the connector meaning 'at' or 'to' in French rather than 'of', and nationalities stay lowercase.
Oui, bien sûr. C'est dommage.

'Yes, of course. It is a pity.' Closing with a two-word expression where the final word looks like 'damage' gives the everyday way to say 'what a shame'. Now let's listen to the whole scene again at normal speed, and see how much more you catch.

C'est un art dramatique puissant.

Il fait chanter toute son équipe.

S'il y a un problème, dis-le.
Hartman a choisi quelqu'un d'autre?

Il pense à une actrice américaine.
Oui, bien sûr. C'est dommage.
Although Mathias tries to shield Isabelle from disappointment, the star's curiosity is sparked by the elusive director. See you next time!
Bonne journée!
